title: Survey Reveals Physicists Disagree on Universe's Biggest Mysteries
summary: What if the experts can't agree on how the universe works? That's exactly what the largest global survey of physicists ever conducted has revealed. Researchers found surprisingly little consensus on fundamental questions — from dark matter and black holes to the challenge of reconciling Einstein's theory of gravity with quantum mechanics. Even the standard model of cosmology, known as ΛCDM (Lambda Cold Dark Matter), failed to win majority support. That may reflect recent findings from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), which hinted that dark energy could change over time — a possibility that conflicts with the standard model's assumption that it stays constant. Across all questions, only two received majority agreement. One concerned the Big Bang. Despite how it's often portrayed, 68% of physicists said the Big Bang doesn't necessarily represent the beginning of time. Instead, it describes how the universe developed from an extremely hot, dense state — not whether time had an absolute start. Dark matter was another area of deep division. Only 17% favored the idea that it's made of undiscovered low-mass particles. Another 12% supported modifying the theory of gravity. The largest single group, 21%, favored some combination of explanations. Quantum gravity — the effort to describe gravity using quantum mechanics — was similarly divided, with no dominant approach after decades of work. So is this disagreement a problem? Niayesh Afshordi of the Perimeter Institute sees it as a sign of opportunity. "Scientific truth is not decided by a vote," he says. "But consensus, or its absence, tells us where the evidence feels settled and where researchers still see room for radically different ideas." He quotes songwriter Leonard Cohen: "There is a crack in everything, that's how the light gets in." The findings suggest that some of the most fundamental questions remain open — leaving room for new discoveries to reshape our understanding.
why_it_matters: Science is often taught as a pile of settled answers, but this survey shows the frontier of physics is a live argument — and students entering the field today could be the ones whose new measurements decide questions that have stayed open for decades.

background_read: Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity (published in the early twentieth century, it describes gravity as the bending of space and time) works beautifully for planets and galaxies, but it clashes with quantum mechanics, the rules that govern particles — and quantum gravity is the long-sought bridge between them.

DESI (the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument) is a real instrument that maps the positions of millions of galaxies to trace how the universe has expanded; its hints that dark energy may change over time would shake the standard cosmological model, which treats dark energy as a fixed quantity.

Dark matter was first suspected because galaxies spin and cluster as if they contained far more mass than their visible stars and gas can explain; that invisible mass is inferred from its gravity, not seen directly, which is exactly why competing explanations survive.

Dark energy entered the picture when astronomers found that the universe's expansion is speeding up rather than slowing down, a discovery that earned a Nobel Prize in Physics — a result that ΛCDM absorbs by assuming a constant 'cosmological constant'.

Niayesh Afshordi works at the Perimeter Institute (a theoretical physics research center in Waterloo, Ontario, Canada), and he quotes the Canadian songwriter Leonard Cohen's line 'There is a crack in everything, that's how the light gets in' to argue that disagreement shows where discovery is still possible.

perspectives.description: A major survey gives researchers a map of where the field is genuinely stuck and where money and talent should go next. For young physicists, the lack of consensus is encouraging: it means the biggest questions, from quantum gravity to dark matter, are still open for their ideas.

Some might read the results as a sign that cosmology is drifting without a shared framework, especially since ΛCDM — the model taught in textbooks — could not win majority support. Others warn that surveys measure opinions, not evidence, so a 'vote' can overstate disagreement or understate progress.

Physics has a long history of living with competing theories until decisive data arrive — quantum mechanics and relativity both coexisted uneasily for decades. The DESI hints about changing dark energy fit that pattern: a new measurement challenges a standard assumption, and the field waits for confirmation before rewriting the model.

The next steps are observational: more galaxy surveys, better particle detectors, and new tests of gravity at cosmic scales could either restore confidence in ΛCDM or replace it. Either outcome would be progress, which is why Afshordi treats disagreement as a sign of where the light can get in.
